justification: Formed a fresh judgement first, then checked the round-2 history. Both comparison pages were re-fetched today: ByteByteGo is a five-bullet qualitative comparison list with no runnable code, no measurements and no citations to primary sources, and its context-switch claim ('context switching is slow for processes, fast for threads') carries no mechanism or numbers; GeeksforGeeks is definitions plus an 11-row comparison table and two unlabelled stock diagrams, also with no code, no measurements and no citations to authoritative sources. This article remains a different tier: ten runnable, verified C# programs, machine-stated timing ranges (not fake precision), two captioned diagrams with accessible title/desc, and a sources list of primary documentation, man pages, runtime source and a peer-reviewed measurement paper cited inline at the point of the claim. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/operating-systems/processes-and-threads.md` passes cleanly (PASS, blocks=20 executed=10), confirmed by running it myself just now. I re-derived complexity/scheduling claims and re-verified two primary sources myself rather than trusting prior rounds: (1) re-fetched https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/context-switches directly -- its exact text is 'The quantum of a thread expired, and another thread with at least the same priority is ready' plus a separate bullet 'A thread with a higher priority has become ready to run.' The article's current wording ('a thread's quantum being spent is only a reason to switch if some other ready thread at that priority *or higher* is waiting for a turn, while a strictly higher-priority thread becoming ready can end a running thread's turn without waiting for its quantum to be spent at all') reproduces that exact two-case distinction accurately and is not a cosmetic rewrite -- it correctly keeps 'at least the same priority' distinct from 'strictly higher,' which is the nuance round 2's article text had collapsed into 'equal-priority' (an AdSense-round-2 finding that also had a technical-accuracy dimension: 'equal-priority' silently narrows and misstates the source's 'at least the same priority'). That is now fixed. (2) Re-fetched https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/about-processes-and-threads and confirmed the article's process/thread attribute lists and the job-object sentence ('a Windows job object manages a group of processes as a unit') match the source ('A job object allows groups of processes to be managed as a unit... Operations performed on the job object affect all processes associated with the job object'). I also checked the git diff between the round-2 commit and the current draft: exactly three paragraphs changed, matching the two round-2 technical minors and the priority nuance, with nothing else touched. Both round-2 technical minors are genuinely fixed, not patched: the orders-of-magnitude sentence now reads 'The pool-to-thread step is roughly one order of magnitude (about eight to twenty times); the thread-to-process step stacks a further two to three orders of magnitude on top of that' -- checking the article's own numbers (8-11 us pool, 85-165 us thread, 24,000-28,000 us process) gives ratios of about 7.7x-20.6x for the first step and about 145x-329x for the second, which is accurately described as 'about eight to twenty times' and 'two to three orders of magnitude' respectively, correcting round 1's original overstatement that round 2 had only partly softened. The AutoResetEvent sentence now says each `Set`/`WaitOne` 'operates on a native OS handle... rather than something the runtime can resolve in user mode alone' instead of round 2's stronger 'reaches into the kernel,' which matches the fix round 2 itself suggested and no longer asserts more than the cited class-reference page supports. I found no new factual error, no unsupported claim, and no citation that does not say what the article attributes to it. With all three open items resolved, code passing, and the content still substantially more rigorous than the top-ranking pages for this query, this clears the 8.5 (MDN/Real Python) anchor with room to spare and is close to the 10 anchor (clearly better than the best existing result); it is not a full 10 because a few summary sentences (e.g. 'A process with 50 ready threads competes as 50 entries') are the writer's own reasonable inference rather than a directly cited fact, which is fine but keeps this just short of flawless.
